problems.title: Min Stack
problems.description:
Design a stack that supports `push`, `pop`, `top` and `getMin`, where every operation must run in O(1) time. `getMin` returns the smallest value currently in the stack.

To make this testable, implement `min_stack(ops)`. `ops` is a list of operations, each a list: `["push", x]`, `["pop"]`, `["top"]` or `["getMin"]`. Apply them in order to an initially empty stack and return a list with one result per operation: `null` for `push` and `pop`, and the returned value for `top` and `getMin`.

`pop`, `top` and `getMin` are only ever called on a non-empty stack.

examples.explanation: After pushing -2, 0, -3 the minimum is -3. Popping removes -3, so the top is 0 and the minimum returns to -2.

constraints: pop, top and getMin are never called on an empty stack
problems.complexity: O(1) time per operation, O(n) space
hints: Knowing the current minimum is easy when you only push. The hard part is what the minimum becomes after a pop.
Store, alongside each element, the minimum of the stack at the moment that element was pushed.

Keep a second stack (or pair each value with its running minimum). Pushing sets the new minimum to `min(x, previous minimum)`; popping removes both entries, restoring the earlier minimum automatically.

problems.title: Implement Queue Using Stacks
problems.description:
Build a first-in-first-out queue using only two stacks. You may only use stack operations: push to the top, pop from the top, look at the top, and check whether a stack is empty.

Implement `queue_with_stacks(ops)`. `ops` is a list of operations: `["push", x]` (enqueue x), `["pop"]` (remove and return the front), `["peek"]` (return the front without removing it) and `["empty"]` (return whether the queue is empty). Return one result per operation: `null` for `push`, the value for `pop` and `peek`, and a boolean for `empty`.

`pop` and `peek` are only called when the queue is non-empty. Aim for amortized O(1) per operation.
constraints: pop and peek are never called on an empty queue
problems.complexity: Amortized O(1) per operation, O(n) space
hints: A single stack reverses order. What happens if you pour one stack into another?
Use an `inbox` stack for pushes and an `outbox` stack for pops and peeks.
Only when `outbox` is empty, move every element from `inbox` to `outbox`. Each element moves at most once, which gives amortized O(1).

problems.title: Next Greater Element (Circular)
problems.description:
You are given a circular array `nums`: after the last element, the scan continues from the first element again. For every index `i`, find the first element strictly greater than `nums[i]` that you meet when walking forward (wrapping around at most once). If no such element exists, the answer for that index is `-1`.

Return an array `answer` of the same length.

examples.explanation: For the last 1 the scan wraps around and finds 2. The 2 has nothing larger anywhere, so it gets -1.

hints: Brute force scans up to n elements per index. Can elements that are already answered be skipped?
A monotonic stack of indices whose next greater element is still unknown works well. Each new value resolves every smaller value waiting on the stack.
Iterate `2n` positions using `i % n`. Only push indices during the first pass; in both passes pop while the stack top is smaller than the current value and assign it.

problems.title: Remove K Digits
problems.description:
You are given a string `num` holding a non-negative integer and an integer `k`. Remove exactly `k` digits so that the remaining number is as small as possible, and return it as a string.

The result must not contain leading zeros, except that if the result is zero it must be the single character `"0"`.

examples.explanation: Removing 4, 3 and 2 leaves 1219, the smallest possible.
Removing the 1 leaves 0200, which becomes 200 after stripping leading zeros.

constraints: num has no leading zeros unless it is "0"
hints: Compare removing a digit early versus late. Which position matters most for the size of the number?
Greedy: the first digit that is larger than the digit after it is the best one to delete. A monotonic stack finds it efficiently.

Scan left to right; while `k > 0` and the stack top is greater than the current digit, pop and decrement `k`. If `k` remains after the scan, drop digits from the end. Finally strip leading zeros and return `"0"` for an empty result.

problems.title: Decode String
problems.description:
An encoded string uses the rule `k[text]`, meaning `text` is repeated exactly `k` times. Rules can be nested. Decode the string and return the result.

The input is always well formed: brackets match, `k` is a positive integer (possibly several digits), and digits only appear as repeat counts. Letters outside brackets are copied as is.
constraints: s contains lowercase letters, digits and the characters `[` and `]`
The decoded length is at most 10^4
hints: Handle the innermost brackets first. What data structure naturally gives you the most recent open bracket?
Use a stack. When you meet `[`, save the text built so far and the pending repeat count, then start fresh.
On `]`, pop the saved text and count, and set `current = saved + current * count`. Accumulate multi-digit counts as `num = num * 10 + digit`.

problems.title: Simplify Path
problems.description:
Given an absolute Unix-style file path, return its canonical form.

Rules: the path starts with `/`. A single `.` means the current directory and is ignored. `..` moves up one directory (at the root it stays at the root). Multiple consecutive slashes count as one. Any other run of characters, including names like `...`, is an ordinary directory name.

The canonical path starts with a single `/`, separates directories with a single `/`, and does not end with a `/` unless it is the root `/` itself.

examples.explanation: a/./b becomes a/b, then two .. cancel b and a, then c is entered.

constraints: path consists of letters, digits, `.`, `/` and `_`
path is a valid absolute path
hints: Split the path on `/` and think about each piece independently.
A stack of directory names mirrors where you currently are. `..` pops, a normal name pushes.
Ignore empty pieces and `.`. For `..`, pop only if the stack is non-empty. At the end, join the stack with `/` and prefix a single `/`.

problems.title: Basic Calculator with Brackets
problems.description:
Evaluate an arithmetic expression given as a string `s`. It contains non-negative integers, the operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, parentheses `(` and `)`, and optional spaces.

Standard precedence applies: multiplication and division bind tighter than addition and subtraction, and parentheses override everything. Division is integer division that truncates toward zero (so `-7 / 2` is `-3`). There is no unary minus, so `-` always has a left operand, and every intermediate result fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

Return the value of the expression. Do not use `eval` or similar.

examples.explanation: Spaces are ignored. 5 / 2 is 2, so the total is 3 + 2 = 5.

constraints: s is a valid expression and no division by zero occurs
hints: First solve it without parentheses: keep a stack of terms, applying `*` and `/` immediately to the last term and deferring `+`/`-`.
A parenthesized group is just a smaller instance of the same problem that produces a single number.

Write a recursive helper `parse(i)` that evaluates from index `i` until `)` or the end and returns `(value, next_index)`. On `(`, call it recursively and use the returned value as the current number. Truncate division toward zero by using the sign and absolute values.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle
problems.description:
A singly linked list may contain a cycle: some node's `next` pointer leads back to an earlier node. Decide whether the list has a cycle.

The list is described by two arguments: `values`, the node values in order, and `pos`, the 0-based index of the node that the last node's `next` points back to, or `-1` if the last node points to nothing. Build the nodes inside your function and detect the cycle by pointer traversal; the index `pos` must not be used in the detection itself.

Return `true` if the list has a cycle, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: The tail (value -4) links back to the node at index 1, so the list loops.

constraints: pos is -1 or a valid index into values
hints: Remembering every visited node works, but costs extra memory. Can two pointers moving at different speeds help?
Floyd's tortoise and hare: a slow pointer moves one step, a fast pointer moves two.
If the fast pointer ever reaches the end (`None`), there is no cycle. If fast ever equals slow, a cycle exists.

problems.title: Middle of the Linked List
problems.description:
Given the values of a singly linked list as an array `head`, return the values of the list starting from its middle node to the end, as an array.

If the list has two middle nodes (an even number of nodes), use the second one. The list is given as a plain array of node values in order. Build the nodes yourself inside the function (or work directly with indices) - there is no node class provided.

examples.explanation: With six nodes the middle nodes are 3 and 4; the second one (4) is chosen.

hints: You could count the nodes first and then walk half way, but there is a one-pass approach.
Use two pointers: one moves one node at a time, the other two nodes at a time.
When the fast pointer cannot advance further, the slow pointer is at the middle (the second middle for even lengths). Collect values from there to the end.

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
problems.description:
Given the values of a singly linked list as an array `head` and an integer `n`, remove the `n`-th node counting from the end of the list (the last node is `n = 1`) and return the values of the resulting list as an array. The list is given as a plain array of node values in order. Build the nodes yourself inside the function (or work directly with indices) - there is no node class provided.

Try to do it in a single pass over the list.

examples.explanation: The 2nd node from the end is 4, so it is removed.

hints: Finding the node needs the length, or a trick that avoids computing it.
Use two pointers that are `n` nodes apart. When the leading one reaches the end, the trailing one is just before the node to delete.

Add a dummy node before the head so that removing the first node needs no special case. Advance `fast` by `n + 1` steps from the dummy, then move both until `fast` is `None`, and finally set `slow.next = slow.next.next`.

problems.title: Reorder List
problems.description:
A list `L0 -> L1 -> ... -> L(n-1)` must be rearranged into `L0 -> L(n-1) -> L1 -> L(n-2) -> L2 -> ...`, alternating between the front and the back. Node values may not be modified; only the order of nodes changes. The list is given as a plain array of node values in order. Build the nodes yourself inside the function (or work directly with indices) - there is no node class provided. Return the values of the reordered list as an array.

Aim for O(1) extra space beyond the nodes themselves.

examples.explanation: Front and back alternate: 1, 5, 2, 4, then the middle node 3 remains.

hints: The new order interleaves the first half with the reversed second half.
Split the list in the middle with slow/fast pointers, then reverse the second half in place.
Merge the two halves by alternating nodes: take one from the first half, then one from the reversed second half. Cut the first half's tail so it ends cleanly.

problems.title: Add Two Numbers (Linked Lists)
problems.description:
Two non-negative integers are stored as linked lists of digits in **reverse order**, so the first node holds the ones digit. Each list is given as an array of digits. Add the two numbers and return the sum in the same format: an array of digits, ones digit first. The list is given as a plain array of node values in order. Build the nodes yourself inside the function (or work directly with indices) - there is no node class provided.

The numbers have no leading zeros, except the number zero itself, which is `[0]`. The numbers can be far too long to fit in any integer type, so add digit by digit with a carry.

examples.explanation: 342 + 465 = 807, written backwards as [7,0,8].

constraints: No leading zeros except for the number 0 itself
problems.complexity: O(max(m, n)) time, O(max(m, n)) space for the output
hints: Because the lists are already least-significant digit first, you can add exactly like on paper.
Walk both lists together, summing the two digits plus a carry. The new digit is `sum % 10` and the new carry is `sum // 10`.
Keep looping while either list has nodes or the carry is non-zero, so a final carry such as 5 + 5 = 10 adds an extra digit. Treat a missing node as 0.

problems.title: Palindrome Linked List
problems.description:
Given the values of a singly linked list as an array `head`, return `true` if the sequence reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise `false`. The list is given as a plain array of node values in order. Build the nodes yourself inside the function (or work directly with indices) - there is no node class provided.

Copying the values into an array and comparing is easy; try to solve it with O(1) extra space by reversing half of the list in place.
hints: You need to compare the first half with the second half read backwards.
Find the middle with slow/fast pointers, then reverse the second half in place.
Walk from the head and from the reversed half simultaneously, comparing values. Stop when the reversed half runs out; the middle node of an odd-length list needs no comparison.

problems.title: Integer Square Root
problems.description: Given a non-negative integer `x`, return the largest integer `r` such that `r * r <= x` (the square root rounded down). Do not use a built-in exponent or square-root function.

examples.explanation: The square root of 8 is about 2.83, which rounds down to 2.

hints: The answer is somewhere between 0 and x. Which part of that range can you rule out each step?
The predicate `mid * mid <= x` is true for small `mid` and false for large `mid`. Binary search for the boundary.
Search `lo=0, hi=x`; if `mid * mid <= x` record `mid` as a candidate and move `lo = mid + 1`, otherwise `hi = mid - 1`. Return the last candidate.

problems.title: First Bad Version
problems.description:
Versions `1..n` of a product were released one after another. From some version onward every release is bad (a bad version breaks all later ones). You can ask a function `isBadVersion(v)` whether version `v` is bad, but each call is expensive, so make as few calls as possible.

Here the oracle is built in: you are given `n` and `bad`, the first bad version, and `isBadVersion(v)` is simply `v >= bad`. Write your solution so that it only learns about versions through that predicate, and return the first bad version using O(log n) calls.

examples.explanation: Versions 4 and 5 are bad; 4 is the first.

hints: Versions are ordered good...good bad...bad. What does that give you when you test the middle version?
If the middle is bad, the answer is at the middle or to its left; otherwise it is strictly to the right.
Keep `lo = 1, hi = n`. While `lo < hi`, set `mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2`; if bad, `hi = mid`, else `lo = mid + 1`. Return `lo`.

problems.title: Search a 2D Matrix
problems.description:
You are given an `m x n` integer matrix with two properties: each row is sorted in non-decreasing order, and the first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row. Return `true` if `target` is in the matrix, otherwise `false`.

Your solution should run in O(log(m * n)) time.

examples.explanation: 13 falls between 11 and 16 and does not appear.

hints: Because each row continues where the previous one ended, the whole matrix is one long sorted sequence.
Imagine the matrix flattened into an array of length `m * n`. You can binary search that virtual array without building it.
For a virtual index `k`, the value is `matrix[k // n][k % n]`. Run an ordinary binary search on `0 .. m*n - 1`.

problems.title: Find the Peak Element
problems.description:
An array `nums` is guaranteed to have exactly one peak: it strictly increases up to some index and then strictly decreases (either part may be empty). A peak is an element strictly greater than its neighbours, where the positions before the first and after the last element count as negative infinity.

Return the index of the peak. An O(log n) solution is expected.

examples.explanation: 3 is greater than both neighbours, at index 1.

constraints: nums strictly increases and then strictly decreases, so exactly one peak exists
hints: A linear scan works. What does the comparison of two adjacent elements tell you about which side the peak is on?
If `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]` you are on an uphill slope, so a peak lies to the right.
Binary search with `lo = 0, hi = n - 1` while `lo < hi`: if `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]` set `lo = mid + 1`, else `hi = mid`. When they meet, that index is the peak.

problems.title: Search Insert Position
problems.description: Given a sorted array of distinct integers `nums` and a `target`, return the index of `target` if it is present. Otherwise return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted. Your algorithm must run in O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: 2 would sit between 1 and 3, at index 1.

constraints: nums is sorted ascending with distinct values
hints: If the target is present you return its index; if not, the answer is the count of elements smaller than the target.
That is the first index whose value is `>= target`, i.e. a lower bound.
Binary search with `lo = 0, hi = n`: if `nums[mid] < target`, `lo = mid + 1`, else `hi = mid`. Return `lo`.

problems.title: Split Array Largest Sum
problems.description: Split the array `nums` of non-negative integers into exactly `k` non-empty contiguous subarrays so that the largest subarray sum is as small as possible. Return that minimised largest sum.

examples.explanation: Split as [7,2,5] and [10,8]; the larger sum is 18, and no split does better.

hints: Instead of searching for the split, guess the answer: can the array be split into at most `k` parts, each with sum at most `limit`?
That feasibility check is a greedy scan: keep adding elements to the current part until the limit would be exceeded, then start a new part. Feasibility is monotonic in `limit`.
Binary search `limit` between `max(nums)` (smallest possible) and `sum(nums)` (one part). If the greedy count of parts is `<= k`, try a smaller limit; otherwise a larger one.

problems.title: Capacity to Ship Packages
problems.description:
A conveyor belt carries packages with weights `weights[i]` that must be shipped **in the given order**. Each day, you load packages onto the ship in order, never exceeding the ship's weight capacity, and ship them. A package cannot be split or skipped.

Return the smallest ship capacity that allows all packages to be shipped within `days` days.
hints: The capacity must be at least the heaviest package, and never needs to exceed the total weight.
For a fixed capacity you can count the days needed with a single greedy pass. More capacity never needs more days.
Binary search the capacity between `max(weights)` and `sum(weights)`: if the days needed are `<= days`, shrink the upper bound; otherwise raise the lower bound.

problems.title: Can Attend All Meetings
problems.description:
You are given a list of meeting time intervals `intervals`, where `intervals[i] = [start, end]`. Return `true` if one person could attend every meeting, that is, no two meetings overlap in time, otherwise `false`.

A meeting that ends at the exact moment another one starts does not overlap with it. The input is not necessarily sorted.

examples.explanation: The meetings [0,30] and [5,10] overlap.

problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
hints: If the meetings were in chronological order, which pairs would you need to compare?
Sort by start time. Only neighbouring meetings can conflict once sorted.
After sorting, return `false` as soon as some meeting starts before the previous one ends (`start < previous_end`). Equal values are fine.

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.description: Given a list of intervals `[start, end]`, return the minimum number of intervals you must remove so that the remaining intervals do not overlap. Intervals that merely touch (one ends exactly where another begins) do not overlap.

examples.explanation: Removing [1,3] leaves [1,2], [2,3], [3,4], which do not overlap.

problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
hints: Removing the fewest intervals is the same as keeping the most intervals that are mutually compatible.
Classic activity selection: sort by end time and greedily keep the interval that finishes earliest.
Sort by end. Track the end of the last kept interval. If the next start is `>=` that end, keep it; otherwise count a removal.

problems.title: Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons
problems.description:
Balloons are taped to a wall that we treat as a number line. Balloon `i` spans horizontally from `points[i][0]` to `points[i][1]` (inclusive). An arrow shot straight up from position `x` bursts every balloon with `start <= x <= end`, and keeps travelling.

Return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all the balloons.

examples.explanation: An arrow at x=6 bursts [2,8] and [1,6]; another at x=12 bursts [10,16] and [7,12].

problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
hints: One arrow can burst a group of balloons only if they all share a common point.
Sort the balloons by their right end. Shooting at the right end of the first balloon bursts the most others that start before it.
Keep the position of the latest arrow. For each balloon in sorted order, if its start is greater than the arrow position, you need a new arrow at this balloon's end.

problems.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
problems.description:
Given an `m x n` integer matrix, whenever an element is `0`, set its entire row and its entire column to `0`. Return the resulting matrix.

A zero that appears because of this rule must not trigger further changes: only the zeros present in the original matrix matter. A solution using O(1) extra space is possible by using the matrix's own first row and column as markers.

examples.explanation: The zeros at (0,0) and (0,3) clear rows and columns 0 and 3; row 0 becomes all zeros.

problems.complexity: O(m * n) time, O(1) extra space
hints: First record which rows and columns contain a zero, then do a second pass to clear them. Why can't you clear while scanning?
To avoid extra arrays, store the markers in the first row and first column of the matrix itself.

Remember separately whether the first row and the first column originally contained a zero. Mark with the inner cells, zero out the inner cells according to the markers, and finally clear the first row/column if needed.

problems.title: Game of Life
problems.description:
The Game of Life is played on an `m x n` grid where each cell is alive (`1`) or dead (`0`). Each cell interacts with its eight neighbours (horizontal, vertical, diagonal). The next generation is computed for all cells simultaneously using these rules:

1. A live cell with fewer than two live neighbours dies.
2. A live cell with two or three live neighbours stays alive.
3. A live cell with more than three live neighbours dies.
4. A dead cell with exactly three live neighbours becomes alive.

Given the current `board`, return the board after one step. The update is simultaneous, so you must not let already-updated cells influence the neighbour counts of cells that come later. Try to do it in place with O(1) extra space by encoding transitions in the cell values.

examples.explanation: A vertical bar of three cells turns into a horizontal bar.

problems.complexity: O(m * n) time, O(1) extra space
hints: Computing the new value directly in place corrupts neighbours' counts. How could a cell remember both its old and its new state?
Use extra codes: `2` means 'was alive, now dead' and `3` means 'was dead, now alive'. A neighbour counts as previously alive if its value is 1 or 2.
Pass one: for each cell count previously-alive neighbours and assign the transition codes. Pass two: map `2 -> 0` and `3 -> 1`.

problems.title: Valid Sudoku
problems.description:
Determine whether a partially filled 9 x 9 Sudoku board is valid. Only the filled cells are checked, according to these rules:

- Each row contains the digits `1-9` at most once.
- Each column contains the digits `1-9` at most once.
- Each of the nine 3 x 3 sub-boxes contains the digits `1-9` at most once.

The board is given as a 9 x 9 array of single-character strings: `"1"` to `"9"` for filled cells and `"."` for empty cells. A valid board does not have to be solvable; you only validate the digits already placed.

examples.explanation: Changing the top-left cell to 8 duplicates the 8 in its 3 x 3 box (and in its column).

hints: You need to detect duplicates in three different groupings of the same cells.
Keep a set of seen digits for every row, every column and every box.
The box index of cell `(r, c)` is `(r // 3) * 3 + c // 3`. For each filled cell, if its digit is already in the row, column or box set return `false`; otherwise add it to all three.

problems.title: Number of 1 Bits
problems.description: Given a non-negative integer `n` (it fits in 32 unsigned bits), return the number of `1` bits in its binary representation (also called the Hamming weight).

examples.explanation: 11 is 1011 in binary, which has three 1 bits.

problems.complexity: O(k) time where k is the number of set bits, O(1) space
hints: Looking at every one of the 32 bits works. Can you jump straight from one set bit to the next?
The expression `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit of `n`.
Repeat `n &= n - 1` and count iterations until `n` becomes 0.

problems.title: Counting Bits
problems.description:
Given an integer `n`, return an array `ans` of length `n + 1` where `ans[i]` is the number of `1` bits in the binary representation of `i`.

Counting each number separately takes O(n log n). Try to do it in a single pass, O(n), by reusing earlier answers.
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the output
hints: Look at the binary forms of 0..8 and compare each number to a smaller one.
Shifting `i` right by one drops its last bit. So the count for `i` is the count for `i >> 1` plus that last bit.
`ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`, filled in increasing order of `i` with `ans[0] = 0`.

problems.title: Single Number
problems.description:
Every element of the integer array `nums` appears exactly twice, except for one element that appears exactly once. Find and return that single element.

Your solution must run in linear time and use only constant extra space.

examples.explanation: 1 and 2 each appear twice; 4 is left.

constraints: Every element appears twice except one
hints: A hash map of counts works but uses O(n) memory. Is there an operation under which duplicates vanish?
XOR has the properties `a ^ a = 0` and `a ^ 0 = a`, and it is commutative and associative.
XOR every element together. All pairs cancel and the remaining value is the single number.

problems.title: Power Function
problems.description:
Implement `my_pow(x, n)` that returns `x` raised to the integer power `n`, without using the built-in power operator or function. `n` may be negative, in which case the result is `1 / x^|n|`.

Return the result rounded to 5 decimal places. Multiplying `x` by itself `n` times is too slow for large `n`; use exponentiation by squaring so only O(log |n|) multiplications are needed.

examples.explanation: 2.1 cubed is 9.261.

hints: x^n can be computed from x^(n/2): if you square the half-power you get the whole thing.
Square the base each step and halve the exponent; whenever the exponent is odd, also multiply the result by the current base.
Handle a negative `n` by replacing `x` with `1 / x` and `n` with `-n` up front (Python integers and JS numbers both handle `-2^31` safely). Round the final answer to 5 decimals.

problems.title: Happy Number
problems.description:
Start with a positive integer `n` and repeatedly replace it with the sum of the squares of its digits. If this process eventually reaches `1`, the number is happy. Otherwise it loops forever in a cycle that never includes `1`.

Return `true` if `n` is a happy number, and `false` if it is not.
problems.complexity: O(log n) time per step, O(1) space with cycle detection
hints: Try a few numbers by hand. The sequence either hits 1 or starts repeating.
Detecting repetition is the key. A set of seen values works, but Floyd's cycle detection needs no extra memory.
Define `next(n)` as the digit-square sum. Run slow = next(slow) and fast = next(next(fast)) until `fast == 1` (happy) or `slow == fast` (cycle without 1).
